outline.h2: What does MVP design cover, and what is a minimum viable product not?
outline.answerHint: MVP design is the work of turning one product hypothesis into 3–5 tested core user flows, high-fidelity screens and a starter design system that a startup's developers can build. A minimum viable product is a working product real users rely on; it is not a clickable prototype, not an investor demo and not version 1 with fewer coats of paint.
points: Intro before this H2 (fill-in hypothesis intro, see variety): first sentence carries the keyword (carrier above) and shows the blank sentence. Second paragraph: what the post gives (6 steps: hypothesis, cut list, flows, screens, 5-user test, handoff) and that it ends with a realistic 4–8 week plan. UP link in the first 300 words: anchor 'UI UX design for startups' -> /services/ui-ux-design-services-for-startups/.

Expand 'minimum viable product (MVP)' at first use and keep 'product' or 'startup' next to MVP here (disambiguation from the Model-View-Presenter software pattern, which page 1 shows for 'mvp design'). Use 'minimum viable product design' once. Name the parent 'product design'.
Cite Eric Ries for the MVP idea (The Lean Startup; build-measure-learn) in our own words, one or two sentences, link theleanstartup.com principles page.

Table, introduced by one sentence: clickable prototype vs investor demo vs MVP vs full product. Columns: who uses it, does it run on real data, what it proves, typical fidelity. Investor demo row in the industry page's wording ('a clickable prototype of the next 2 releases a funding round pays for'). Full product row: the hub's comparison with digital product design is NOT repeated; just say an MVP stops before product-market fit is proven. Visual 1 is this table.
Do NOT write a discovery-vs-MVP section (is-discovery-phase-worth-it owns 'framing it as discovery phase vs MVP sets up a false choice'). Do not link that post (another silo).

outline.h2: Step 1: how do you turn the idea into one MVP hypothesis?
outline.answerHint: MVP design starts with one sentence that names the startup's target user, the job they hire the product for, the one core user flow the MVP offers and the riskiest assumption it tests. Then pick one success signal, such as the share of sign-ups who complete the core action in the first session.
points: Return to the intro's blank sentence and fill it with an illustrative example (invented startup, label it illustrative), e.g. a scheduling tool for independent physiotherapists.
Jobs to be Done: one sentence of definition, then the hub figure: 5–8 Jobs to be Done interviews about the tool or workaround each user relies on today. 'interview count' attribute printed here.

Success signal attribute: one activation event per hypothesis, written so developers can track it later (hub benefit wording: activation rate = share of early users who complete the core action in the first session). No uplift figure.
Value proposition: the hypothesis tests 1 value proposition (hub wording). One sentence.
Body carrier: 'Knowing how to design an MVP starts with what to leave out, and the hypothesis decides that.' (one literal keyword use).

outline.h2: Step 2: how do you cut the feature list down to 3–5 MVP flows?
outline.answerHint: Cut every feature that the core user flow does not need, that does not test the MVP hypothesis, or that a person on the startup team can do by hand for the first users. What survives is usually 3–5 flows, for example sign-up, the core action and payment.
points: Present the three-question cut test as our working rule (label it as our practice, not a statistic). Show it on an illustrative 12-item feature list: keep / do by hand / later.
Concierge MVP: define in one sentence (a person delivers the service by hand behind a simple interface) and use it for the 'do by hand' column; e.g. manual invoicing before automated billing.
Flow count attribute: hub '3–5 flows the MVP needs… sign-up, the core action and payment'.

Must-keep items an MVP cannot cut, from the industry page: sign-up consent and data deletion where GDPR/CCPA apply, and an in-app delete-account flow for iOS apps that offer account creation (Apple App Store Review Guideline 5.1.1(v)). Short ul.
Visual 2: feature cut sheet (see visuals). Do NOT use RICE (owned by ux-strategy-roadmap) or a scored yes/no flow (is-discovery-phase-worth-it); this is a three-column sort.

Lead moment 1: founders defend every feature they wrote; an outside facilitator in a 5-day design sprint forces the cut in a day (hub sprint step: 'decide on 1 direction'). One sentence, no claims about other clients.

outline.h2: Step 3: how do you map each core user flow and its states?
outline.answerHint: Map each core user flow of the MVP from the entry point to the success state before designing a screen, then add the empty, loading, error and first-run states the startup's first users will actually see.
points: Map in FigJam (one sentence); each step is a box, each decision a diamond; the success state is the activation event from step 1.
Empty states: define in one sentence; first users always see empty lists and dashboards, so each empty state tells the user the next action.
Error states for the payment and sign-up flows; first-run state (onboarding) in one line each.
Visual 3: core flow map with states (see visuals).
MVP UX design carrier sentence here (secondary).

outline.h2: How to design an MVP's screens: low-fidelity wireframes first, then UI
outline.answerHint: Design the MVP's screens in two passes: low-fidelity wireframes for every screen in the core user flow, then high-fidelity UI only after interviews and a first test confirm the flow. The startup gets a starter design system of tokens and 20–30 core components, not a full design system.
points: Step 4 of 6. Screen fidelity attribute: wireframes first (grey boxes, real copy), UI after 5–8 interviews confirm the problem (reconciles the industry FAQ on pre-seed teams, see siteFacts.conflicts).
MVP UI design carrier sentence (secondary).

Platform rules: Apple Human Interface Guidelines 44×44 pt and Material Design 3 48×48 dp hit targets (hub); WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 contrast for body text and 24×24 CSS px minimum target (industry page; cite W3C Understanding 2.5.8 and 1.4.3). Attributes 'touch target size' and 'contrast ratio' printed here. Visual 4: spec card.

Starter design system: design tokens (colour, typography, spacing; one-sentence definition of 'design tokens') + component count 20–30 core components, e.g. buttons, inputs and cards (hub). Never call it a full design system.
Lead moment 2: the starter design system is where MVPs usually save or lose engineering time later; we build it inside the UI step (hub step 'UI design and prototype, 5–12 days'). One sentence.

outline.h2: Step 5: how do you test the MVP design with 5 users before code?
outline.answerHint: Test the clickable prototype of the MVP's core user flow with 5 target users before engineers write production code: give each user the flow's main task, watch where they stall, record a System Usability Scale score, and change the design before the startup builds it.
points: Test participants attribute: 5 users per round (hub). Cite Jakob Nielsen, 'Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users' (NN/g, 2000) for the reasoning, in our own words; one round finds the biggest problems, then fix and test again.
Tools: clickable Figma prototype tested in Maze (hub). One sentence on moderated sessions over video when the flow is complex.
Write 3 task prompts for the illustrative example (start from a goal, never name the button).

System Usability Scale: 10 questions, scored 0–100; cite MeasuringU (Jeff Sauro) for the average of 68. Fact-checker: confirm on measuringu.com. Do not invent a pass threshold; say a score below the average flags the flow for another round.
Decision after the round: fix and retest / move to handoff / revisit the hypothesis. Plain ul; no flowchart (variety).
Visual 5: 5-user test plan card.

outline.h2: Step 6: what should the MVP design hand to developers?
outline.answerHint: The MVP design hands developers annotated Figma files for every screen and state in the core user flows, the starter design system's tokens and components, the success-signal event to track, and a short list of open questions, so the startup's engineers build what was tested.
points: Developer handoff: hub 'developers receive annotated Figma files'. Figma Dev Mode (one sentence: the Figma view where developers inspect measurements, tokens and code snippets; fact-checker to confirm wording on figma.com).

Handoff pack as a checklist (visual 6 + its text panel): screens with states, flow map, tokens and components, accessibility notes (targets, contrast, focus order), analytics events for the success signal, copy deck, open questions and what was cut for later.
Carrier with literal keyword: 'The last part of how to design an MVP is the part most guides skip: what the developers receive.'
Stay silent on whether we build the MVP (siteFacts.conflicts).

Founder time attribute: 2 review sessions of 45 minutes per week + Figma comment answers within 1 working day (industry page), and 2–3 hours per day during the remote sprint (hub FAQ).

outline.h2: Which MVP design mistakes cause the most rework after launch?
outline.answerHint: The MVP design mistakes that cause the most rework are designing screens before the core user flow, polishing UI before the startup has tested the flow with users, skipping empty and error states, and handing developers screens without tokens or components.
points: 5–6 reasoned bullets (mistake + why it costs rework), each tied back to a step above. Our practice, not statistics.
Include 'designing for every platform at once': platforms are a hub price driver; pick the platform where the core job happens first.
Include 'no success signal defined', so the launch cannot tell the team anything.

Close the section with the hub 'when to hire' deep link: /services/ui-ux-design-services-for-startups/#when-should-a-startup-hire-ui-ux-design-services-for-startups, anchor 'signs a startup needs outside MVP design help'. Do not list the hub's 5 situations.
Closing paragraph after this section (before FAQs): carrier 'If you would rather not work out how to design an MVP alone, send us your feature list…' + /contact/ link.

faqs.q: Can you design an MVP without a designer?
faqs.hint: Yes, for the first two steps: founders can write the hypothesis, cut the feature list and sketch flows in FigJam. The risk sits in states, platform rules and testing; one sentence on when a designer pays off (before high-fidelity UI). No invented failure rates.

faqs.q: How many screens does an MVP need?
faqs.hint: Count flows, not screens: 3–5 MVP flows (hub), each with its empty, error and success states. Do not give a screen count (no source).

faqs.q: Should you design the MVP for web or mobile first?
faqs.hint: Design first for the platform where the target user does the core job; a second platform raises scope and price (hub price driver 'number of platforms'). 2 sentences.

faqs.q: Does a no-code MVP still need UX design?
faqs.hint: Yes. No-code tools change who builds the product, not the flows, states and test the user meets. 2 sentences, no tool comparison.

faqs.q: How much does MVP design cost?
faqs.hint: One intent, one answer: $25,000–$60,000 for a 4–8 week startup engagement on this site, depending on flows, platforms, research depth and the starter design system scope; link the hub cost section. Never quote competitor ranges.
